en: Homage to the glorious Hevajra! Having prostrated with my body—the nectarine, essential nature of all Buddhas—for the sake of awakening, [I praise] that which is free from worldly conduct, consisting of the Victors, eternally arisen, all-pervading, beyond duality, stainless, the bliss of the non-sensory, omniscient, and thus supreme; peaceful, the mind that is the mind of no-mind, non-inert, the faculty of all senses, and present everywhere.
(1) The eight faces of the Lord have destroyed the arising of the eight qualities; the sixteen hands are the emptinesses and compassion, as well as these skull-cups.

The garland of heads on his shoulder is composed of the reality of the fifty excellent phonemes; Akṣobhya is in his crown, along with the half-moon, the vajra, and the garland consisting of skull-cups.

Having bowed to him who, through loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], acts as a liberator, whose conduct is excellent, who stands having crushed the Māras, and for whom the assembly of afflictions and the knowable is his yoga; who wears snakes as his ornaments, a skin as his seal, and a leopard-skin; and for whom the obscurations of Māra and the like are but a trifle because he seeks the welfare of sentient beings—I shall now write this commentary on his secret tantra, which cures diseases.
(3) By the illustrious Vajragarbha, who desires the welfare of all sentient beings and is a lord of the ten stages, this [work] was composed for the sake of yogins attaining the path.
(4) From a great tantra of five hundred thousand [verses], this was extracted into a short tantra;
even in this one of seven hundred and fifty [verses], it is endowed with many vajra-words.
(5) This work, which is considered to consist of six thousand [stanzas], was composed as impelled by Hevajra;
it follows the Root Tantra for the purpose of illuminating the tantra.
(6) Those who will become teachers of the Yogācāra in this age of five corruptions will be promoters of the false path.
(7) Devoid of the commentary, those of evil conduct will teach the minor tantras;
out of greed for the wives and wealth of others, they will be intent on going to hell.
(8) Some will compose commentaries even without the five superknowledges and so forth; out of pride in their dialectical treatises, they are mere mockers of the Yogācāra.
(9) "Having diligently grasped Buddhahood and the state of Vajrasattva through the empowerments,
some men among men will declare themselves to be holders of the Vajra."
(10) All monks who maintain the restraint of ethical discipline are not to be saluted; we, clad in white garments, are ourselves the Vajra-holders on this earth and are thus to be saluted.
(11) Servants, merchants, Śūdras, and those devoted to agricultural labor— these fools, who sell the true Dharma, neither enjoy nor utilize [the fruits of their actions].
(12) Those belonging to Māra’s host will become teachers for their disciples,
concealing under the very guise of the practice of yoga the things they have composed themselves.
(13) They indeed speak of the faults [of the teacher] in order to bring about the abandonment of those faults;
however, the virtues of the teacher are to be accepted, and his faults never at all.
(14) There is no doubt that the disciples will incur the fault of failure here:
[if they serve one who is] merciless, wrathful, cruel, arrogant, greedy, and unrestrained.
(15) A wise person should neither exalt himself nor disparage his teacher or disciple;
they shall by no means teach this statement to their disciples.
(16) One who is merciless, a cultivator of the soil, wrathful, a piercer of vital spots,
cruel, a hater of mendicants, stubborn, and arrogant with false knowledge;
(17) Even one who is greedy, seeking not to enjoy [the fruits of his own merit], yet unrestrained by excessive intoxicants,
is here said to be one who exalts himself and brings faults upon those possessed of virtues.
(18) For the Vajrācārya who has received the supreme consecration is honored at the three times of day by the Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions, who come to him.
(19) Not understanding the intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*) and deluded by mere names,
they will go to the Raurava hell after having committed the rejection of the Lords of Jinas.
(20) He who has been consecrated at the foot of the Bodhi tree by Vajrasattva upon his head,
having obtained the supreme consecration— he is the Vajrācārya Tathāgata.
(21) The worlds that are the bodies of the bodhisattvas of the ten directions—
approaching there at the three times, he is honored by the five aggregates residing therein.
(22) Their world-systems consist of various jewels as their crowns;
by the Buddhas residing therein, that Vajrācārya of yogins is worshipped.
(23) Vairocana is the urine, and Akṣobhya is the semen; Amitābha is the Samaya, and likewise the Teacher is the Holder of the Vajra.
Just as the preceptor is the giver of feces, urine, semen, and the mudrās,
so too is the Vajra-holder the giver of the accomplishments of body, speech, and mind.
(25) Both through the conventional and the ultimate [truth], for the disciples as well as for the yogins,
there is the former and likewise the latter consecration in the maṇḍala and at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

(26) Sandhyābhāṣā is according to the twilight [intention]; it is not otherwise than literal sound. That which is literal sound is of definitive meaning; thus should the Tantra, characterized by the six parameters, be understood.
(27) Those qualities of the Ācārya which have been shown here through conventional usage are also the qualities of Vajrasattva, characterized by the six superknowledges and so forth.
(28) Steadfast, disciplined, wise, patient, upright, and free from deceit;
skilled in the application of mantra and tantra, compassionate, and proficient in the treatises.
(29) An ācārya is one who thoroughly knows the ten principles, is skilled in the work of drawing mandalas, is an expounder of mantras, possesses a serene mind, and has conquered his senses.
(30) A monk endowed with these aforementioned qualities shall be a Vajradhara; neither a novice nor a householder [is so]. Therefore, those two do not possess the ten attributes of a monk.
(31) One endowed with the ten precepts, one joined with the five precepts, and one endowed with ten million precepts— these three are considered not equal to you.
(32) Just as it was proclaimed in the Root Tantra regarding the state of a Vajradhara for a monk, something [further] is now being told for those disciples who propitiate their guru.
(33) Thus requested by Nairātmyā, the Vajrī spoke these words in due order and according to the rule, for the purpose of bestowing the precepts:
Having first bestowed the five precepts together with the poṣadha and so forth,
and the renunciation of the ten unwholesome actions, one should make [the candidate] an upāsaka.
(35) Then, having given the ten precepts, one should make [the candidate] a śrāmaṇera; then, having given the ten million precepts, one should make him a bhikṣu, O observer of vows.
(36) Having understood the Prātimokṣa, and thereafter the Vaibhāṣika doctrine;
having understood the Sūtrānta, and thereafter the Vijñānavāda according to its own nature.
(37) Then, having understood the Madhyamaka, the doctrine of the Perfection of Wisdom,
and having understood all other tantras, Hevajra is subsequently known.
(38) Having emerged from the three vehicles, he abides in the fruit of the single vehicle;
herein, the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Mahāyāna as the third.
(39) For Buddhists, there is no fourth [truth], nor is there a fifth; emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is the cause from the very beginning.

(40) It is the Sage’s view that compassion, arising from his meditative concentration, subsequently brings about the welfare of the world as its fruit; for he who, having accomplished his own purpose, causes the welfare of others to be accomplished is truly wise.
(41) How can one who is himself suffering and poor bestow happiness, sovereignty, and prosperity upon others while striving for the welfare of sentient beings?
(42) As long as the cause is not directly produced by one who seeks the cause and its effect, how could the effect first come into being without a cause?
(43) A second vehicle superior to the Mahāyāna is spoken of here;
it is for the sake of providing rest to those who have strayed from generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth, but not in reality.
(44) I have taught that the emptiness of all phenomena is the way of transcendence;
for that reason, because of transcendence, and furthermore, by the power of one's vow.
(45) There will be a great fruit consisting of compassion that is without objective support; compassion without objective support regarding sentient beings and phenomena is known to be threefold.
(46) It is somewhat effective for the purpose [of practice] in a particular region when it relies upon the qualities of sentient beings;
[it is fully effective] for the perfected Bodhisattvas whose selves abide on the ten stages.
(47) For the Sugatas who have ceased the twelve links [of dependent origination], whose selves abide on all stages, it is taught that their non-referential [wisdom] effects the welfare of the world.
(48) Of whatever kind the cause is, of that very kind is the fruit; for indeed, rice never arises from *kodrava* seeds.

(49) As is the seed, so is the tree; as is the tree, so is the fruit. My word is auspicious in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. From an initial cause accompanied by conceptual construction, there will be a result accompanied by conceptual construction; yet at the end, for all Buddhists, the result of conceptual construction is emptiness.
(51) Now, first, for the sake of purifying the field, one should sow kodrava seeds;
afterwards, once the field has been purified, one sows the rice seed.
(52) It is said that the human state born in the land of action is not a pure field;
birth in the higher realms, arising from the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, is impure.
When the field of human birth is pure, compassion that is without objective support is like a seed sown therein; from that, the wish-fulfilling tree of emptiness arises.
From the wish-fulfilling tree of emptiness, the fruit of non-referential compassion arises for all sentient beings whenever it is thought of; of this there is no doubt.
(55) O beloved, those mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth that have been taught by me are for those whose minds lack the capacity for the profound and sublime dharmas.
In the future, teachers belonging to the host of Māras will teach Buddhahood and the state of Vajrasattva by means of mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth.
(57) Therefore, the monk who is the teacher in the Mahāyāna is known as the Vajra-holder;
he is the one who has fully understood the three vehicles and is the knower of the compendium of the Dharma.
(58) Regarding the Vedas, Siddhāntas, and Yogas composed by Īśvara and others,
as well as the Tantras and Mantras of the Buddhists, there is no distinction with respect to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
(59) That deluded soul who does not understand this would cause his disciples to fall into barrenness; for there is no action without an agent, nor is there any fruit devoid of action.
(60) Mahāmāyā is most fierce, the bringer of the destruction of all beings.

She herself is the creator, she herself is the destroyer, she herself is the king, she herself is the lord. Just as the Māyā of Īśvara is spoken of [as Īśvara] by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) in the Śiva-siddhānta, so too is Janārdana [spoken of] in the Gītā-dharma; he is the tamer of the unsubdued, and he is the protector of the virtuous.
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness here, O Bhārata, and an uprising of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself.
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked, and for the establishment of righteousness, I manifest myself in age after age.
(64) Having thus fully understood all such perverted teachings of the Dharma, Hevajra indeed exhorted me to compose this commentary.
(65) Having bowed to the supreme body—naturally pure, honored by the three worlds, called the Dharma-body, free from the states of pleasure and pain;

to the Enjoyment-body, the teacher; and to the Emanation-body, endowed with various miraculous powers and like an illusion or a magical trick—I shall briefly explain its definitive meaning, the secret speech of the *Laghutantra*.

(66) Here, in this concise *Hevajra*, which is the teaching of the Jina, this [meaning] has not been fully clarified for men. Previously, it was composed by the Buddhas in five hundred thousand verses within the collection of the original tantras;

or else, the attainment of the meaning occurred through commentaries on the *Lakṣābhidhāna*—consisting of one hundred thousand verses multiplied by a thousand—or even in other collections of royal tantras.
(67) He who, devoid of a commentary, would teach a hidden word within a collection of minor tantras, is like one who, lacking eyes, would seek to see the tracks of a long-vanished serpent in water.

The Jinas have taught that not every tantra is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); some are of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). If that which is of interpretable meaning is made manifest by a commentary, then the definitive [meaning] is rendered useless for the sake of awakening.

(68) This entire tantra taught by the Jinas is neither intentional speech (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*) nor non-intentional speech; it is not something other than that which is swift, nor is it something other than that which is swift; it is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and not of interpretable meaning. For the aggregates (*skandha*) here—such as excrement and so forth—are impure, and those aggregates are not deities. Nor are they conceived for the sake of awakening by means of the faces and arms of a deity.

(69) How could that Tantra taught by the Blessed One, such as the *Samāja* and others—which is surrounded by six points and which shatters the pride of scholars and treatises—be accessible through logic?
This non-dual gnosis alone is like a reflection in a mirror; it perceives the three times and is free from the web of conceptual constructions regarding existence and non-existence.

(70) For the Blessed One has taught that there are thirty-two flows of semen in Mahāsukha; likewise, those which have reached the throat, as well as the heart, the navel, and the secret place—what flows are they at the joints of the hands and feet, and at the joints of the fingers of the hands? These were not explained by the Jina to me or to Vajragarbha even in the *Hevajra*.

(71) That which the classes of mendicants call "the word of the ṛṣis" is the Māgadhī language and nothing else; that which belongs to the Blessed One in the Tripiṭaka is, according to the opinion of Sthavira, [in that same language]. This fourfold refuge of the Sage consists of the meaning and so forth, not of the phrasing and so forth; it is a disease for one thing and a medicine for another.

(72) That which consists of the sounds of gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, and others, which is indicative of all phenomena, which simultaneously causes wonder and captivates the world with its parables—this very thing, characterized by refined language (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇā*), is called the "Aryan speech" of the Blessed One beginning with the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). Is this not indeed a marvel for wise people?

(73) That body which is like a supreme Indra-net of all aspects, resembling an illusion, and moving through space, is described by the foolish and the worldly for the sake of awakening as belonging to the Blessed One. It is fashioned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, and it stands together with the aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, and objects. Here, the dull-witted desire to know dependent origination, yet they are taught in other tantras through calculations such as destruction, arising, lunar days, and fixed positions. What greater fool than one who desires curd without milk, or milk without cows—even though it is "cow-derived" (gavya)—is there any fault here in this mandala for one who is devoid of boldness?
(74) [Of the wise:]

(75) By means of Hevajra, this Cakrasaṃvara is to be known as the Four Seats; indeed, by means of the words of Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra is to be known as the Four Seats; this Laghucakrasaṃvara is to be known through the Four Seats; furthermore, the definitive meaning is to be known by the words of the Ādibuddha and the Great Samvaras.
(76) Thus, other tantras should always be understood through other tantras—by means of summaries, detailed explanations, and commentaries—by those who long for the path.
(77) Thus ends the first chapter, the introduction to the Tantra, titled "Praise of the Desired Deity," in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*.
